segments.text: Ala bierze kartkę i czyta: Lampa. Brak. Jan pokazuje rysunek: lampa, strzałka i koło. Ewa patrzy. Jest dzień. Tu jest warsztat. W warsztacie jest stół i okno. Jan pokazuje stół. Na stole leży rysunek.

Tu jest ściana. To jest lista. Lista wisi na ścianie. Ewa pokazuje listę. Jan patrzy: lista, nie kartka. Na kartce jest napis: Brak. Na liście jest pudełko, szuflada i półka. Ala pokazuje papier: półka i szuflada. To jest rysunek. Jan nie bierze papieru. Czyta listę.

Jan pyta: „Czy masz listę?” Ala odpowiada: „Nie mam listy. Mam kartkę. Lista jest na ścianie.” Jan pokazuje listę. Ala kładzie kartkę tu. Ewa pokazuje rysunek: półka i szuflada. Jan nie bierze rysunku. Pokazuje listę: pudełko, szuflada, półka. Ala czyta listę.
„Czy rozumiesz? Tu jest lista. Tam jest kartka.”

Jan nie otwiera pudełka. Pokazuje dno. W pudełku nie ma lampy. Ewa pokazuje listę na ścianie. Ala czyta: W pudełku. Potem pokazuje szufladę.

grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: Warsztat → w warsztacie. Półka → na półce. Lampa stoi na półce.
grammar.note_en:
The locative is a noun case used after certain prepositions. Here it names a static place: where something is, stands, lies or hangs. W usually means “in” in these examples; na means “on”. W warsztacie is “in the workshop”, na stole “on the table”, and na półce “on the shelf”. A preposition goes before its noun, and the noun takes a locative form. This chapter teaches only the demonstrated singular forms and only these static uses of w and na. It does not teach every preposition or every meaning of w and na.

Compare the naming form with the place phrase: warsztat → w warsztacie (“workshop → in the workshop”); ściana → na ścianie (“wall → on the wall”); podłoga → na podłodze (“floor → on the floor”); półka → na półce (“shelf → on the shelf”); stół → na stole (“table → on the table”); szuflada → w szufladzie (“drawer → in the drawer”); pudełko → w pudełku (“box → in the box”); okno → w oknie (“window → in the window”); rysunek → na rysunku (“drawing → in/on the drawing”); kartka → na kartce (“note/sheet → on the note/sheet”); lista → na liście (“list → on the list”). Learn each complete phrase, including its preposition. Polish and English do not always select the same preposition: a feature depicted in a drawing is na rysunku, and an entry in a list is na liście. W oknie can identify the window opening or window area; the scene shows light there, not a person standing inside the glass.

There is no single ending to attach to every noun. Several nouns here have -e or -ie with a consonant change: warsztat → warsztacie, ściana → ścianie, podłoga → podłodze, półka → półce, stół → stole, szuflada → szufladzie, okno → oknie, kartka → kartce and lista → liście. Notice the whole spelling, not just the last letter: ł becomes l and ó becomes o in stół → stole. By contrast, pudełko → pudełku keeps ł. Rysunek → rysunku loses the e before k, and takes -u. These examples do not provide a complete declension rule for every Polish noun. The table is a reference of forms actually used, not a paradigm to fill in.

A static place can accompany both presence and absence: W pudełku nie ma lampy means “There is no lamp in the box”. Pudełku is locative after w; lampy is genitive after the absence construction nie ma. The two endings have different jobs in the same sentence. Na półce nie ma lampy means “There is no lamp on the shelf”. The earlier empty lower shelf is still empty; the newly inspected upper shelf is a different place. A place phrase does not by itself move an object. Lampa stoi na półce means “The lamp stands/is standing on the shelf”; it does not mean that someone is putting the lamp onto the shelf. Taking and putting in the story retain the already known bierze lampę / kładzie lampę tu (“takes the lamp / puts the lamp here”). Directional uses of w and na and their other case patterns are outside this chapter.

Stoi means “stands/is standing”, leży means “lies/is lying”, and wisi means “hangs/is hanging”. They are third-person singular forms describing one named person or thing. The box stands upright on the floor; the paper lies flat on the table; the checklist hangs on the wall. Pudełko stoi na podłodze means “The box stands on the floor”; Rysunek leży na stole means “The drawing lies on the table”; Lista wisi na ścianie means “The list hangs on the wall”. These are different physical positions, not interchangeable translations of jest (“is”). This chapter supplies these three forms, not their complete person paradigms. The spatial adverbs wysoko and nisko mean “high up” and “low down”: Półka jest wysoko / Półka jest nisko means “The shelf is high up / The shelf is low down”. An adverb describes the position here; it does not agree with the noun in gender or case. No adjective pattern or comparative such as “higher” is introduced.

Pęknięcie is a noun meaning “a crack”, naming the visible damage in the cable. Widzę pęknięcie means “I see a crack”. The known recognition-only frame To jest cudza lampa means “This is a lamp belonging to someone else”. Ewa repeats her earlier recollection; the owner remains unidentified. You are not asked to produce that adjective here. The old inventory note still reads Lampa. Brak (“Lamp. Missing”). The note still records the earlier absence.
